newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's oil and gas sector outlook bright - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Australia's oil and gas sector outlook bright - analysts.

text.p: Australia's oil and gas sector is poised to perform brightly this year, driven by a 1996 surge in exploration and corporate activity, analysts say.
The Australian Stock Exchange's Energy Index rose 49 percent last year, underpinned by strong oil prices, compared with a rise of about 10 percent in the broader All Ordinaries Index.
"The sector will still do well, even though everybody anticipates that oil prices will come off or show some volatility," said Macquarie Equities Ltd analyst Peter Best.
Exploration hotspots are expected to include the Timor Sea, Papua New Guinea and the Carnarvon Basin off Western Australia.
The sector's two biggest companies Woodside Petroleum Ltd and Santos Ltd planned to drill key wells in the Timor Sea, while developing the region's Laminaria and Elang oil fields.
In PNG, Oil Search Ltd would continue its exploration of the promising Moran oil field, and had received development licences for the Gobe oil field.
Best said the Carnarvon Basin would be a focus for both development and exploration, and remained under-explored.

The energy sector should also be boosted by the improved prospect for gas projects following moves to deregulate the gas sector in Australia, a build-up of infrastructure and a switch to gas-fired power stations.
Fresh takeover activity is expected, with Australian oil and gas companies seen as undervalued when compared with their international counterparts.
"Oil companies have strong oil prices, their cash flows are very strong, they've got a lot of money in the bank," said James Capel Australia Ltd analyst Mario Traviati.
Producers could either pour funds into exploration, with its long lead-times, or buy production. "If there's value at the corporate level, companies will chase that first," he said.
Predators from the U.S. and U.K. made successful bids in 1996 for Ampolex Ltd, Discovery Petroleum NL and Command Petroleum Holdings.
Traviati nominated Petroz NL, Cultus Petroleum NL, Novus Petroleum Ltd and Tap Oil as possible targets, offering solid earnings and strong balance sheets, along with exploration upside.

Petroz, in particular, was seen as a potential target by analysts, given its 14.95 percent interest in the Undan permit, part of the Bayu-Undan oil field in the Timor Gap where a decision on further development is expected around April.
The oil price, and the severity of the Northern Hemisphere winter, would have a big impact on the sector, said Shaw Stockbroking Ltd analyst John Colnan.
A harsh winter could spark a jump in oil prices to US$30 a barrel, and a 1997 average price of US$25 a barrel, he said. "If that's the case, I think there's another 10 or 20 percent in the sector."
However, any fall in the oil price would have a more immediate impact on the larger companies, rather than the smaller explorers which retained the strongest outlook.
"People aren't really buying (smaller companies) for earnings, they are buying them for a roll of the dice and some high potential exploration," said Traviati.
"If the oil price does come back you will see majors slide back with the price, and the performers will be the second liners."
